commonMistakes: Do not say particles in a solid are completely still; they vibrate about fixed positions.
Do not say gas particles have no forces at all; interactions are much weaker except during collisions.
Do not draw different-sized particles merely to represent different states of the same substance.

detailedExplanation: Verified against The Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 Physics Curriculum Outline 2026–27 and aligned to AQA GCSE Physics 8463.

Matter can be modelled as particles in constant motion. In a solid the particles are closely packed in a fixed arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions; in a liquid they remain close together but can move past one another; in a gas they are much farther apart and move rapidly in random directions.

The macroscopic properties of each state follow from the particle model. Solids keep a fixed shape and volume, liquids keep a fixed volume but take the shape of their container, and gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume and are easily compressed.

Heating increases the energy of particles. Where no change of state is occurring, a rise in temperature corresponds to an increase in the average kinetic energy of the particles. During a change of state, energy changes the internal energy and arrangement rather than raising temperature.
Particle diagrams must show spacing and arrangement accurately. Do not draw particles themselves becoming larger when a substance expands; the separation between particles changes.
